interviewQuestions.question: How do you make sure you're narrating enough during a coding interview without rambling?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I follow a simple loop: state the idea, say why it should work, then write the code for that piece before moving to the next idea. That order matters — saying the idea before typing gives the interviewer a chance to redirect me if I'm heading somewhere wrong, while explaining afterward is just a summary of what already happened.

To avoid rambling, I filter what I say through one question: is this a decision or a mechanic? Which data structure I'm using, why this loop bound, why I'm handling an edge case now rather than later — those are decisions and worth a sentence. Variable names, syntax, fixing a typo — those are mechanics, and I stay quiet on them.

A concrete rhythm that's worked for me: a sentence or two before a meaningful block of code, quiet while typing it, then a short check-in like "that handles the empty-list case" before moving on. Continuous narration of every keystroke reads as anxious filler rather than clarity, so I deliberately leave gaps.

I also always name the brute force out loud first, even briefly, before jumping to the better approach — that ten seconds of narration is worth more than most people expect, because it proves I derived the improvement rather than memorized it.

**Testing:** whether you have a concrete, repeatable process for pacing narration, rather than either going silent or narrating everything indiscriminately.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Give an example of narration that's actually useless, and explain why it doesn't help.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
"Now I'm incrementing i" or "this checks if the array is empty" are the classic useless versions — they describe what a line does, which the interviewer can already read directly off the screen. Saying it out loud adds zero information they didn't already have.

The useful version of the same moment says *why*: "I'm incrementing i because we've confirmed this element can't be part of the answer, so it never needs revisiting" tells the interviewer I understand the invariant driving the loop — that this pointer only ever moves forward and why that's safe — not just that I can narrate my own syntax back to them.

I check myself against a simple rule: if what I'm about to say is visible just by reading the line, it's not worth saying. If it's the reasoning that produced the line — an invariant, a rejected alternative, a trade-off — it is.

This distinction matters because interviewers are trying to tell real understanding apart from a candidate who memorized a pattern and is executing it competently but mechanically. Narrating what-not-why gives no signal either way, and can actually read as padding under time pressure.

**Testing:** whether you can tell the difference between narration that's genuinely informative and narration that's just filling silence.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Common mistakes

interviewQuestions.question: An interviewer interrupts you mid-solution with a question that doesn't relate to what you're currently doing. How do you handle it without losing your train of thought?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I answer directly and briefly, then explicitly re-anchor to where I was: something like "good question — yes, because the array's sorted. So, continuing from the pointer at index three..." That re-anchoring sentence costs almost nothing and keeps the thread visible to both of us, instead of leaving the interviewer to ask "so what were you doing?"

If the interruption would genuinely derail a thought I'm mid-way through — say I'm halfway through deriving an invariant — I'll say so directly: "let me finish this thought and I'll come back to that," and I make sure I actually do come back to it rather than letting it drop. That's a legitimate move, not evasive, as long as I follow through.

I treat interruptions as intentional probes sometimes, not just noise — interviewers do this on purpose to see whether I can hold a train of thought under a real interruption, the same way a teammate might ping me mid-focus in a real job. Losing the thread entirely, or answering curtly without returning to context, both read worse than either handling it smoothly or explicitly deferring it.

**Testing:** whether you can maintain coherent narration under a realistic disruption, rather than only in an uninterrupted monologue.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Handling pressure

interviewQuestions.question: As you've gotten more senior, has your approach to narration changed, and if so how?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes — earlier in my career I narrated to prove I understood my own code; now I narrate to make trade-offs and rejected alternatives visible, because that's the signal senior rounds actually weight. A junior-level narration says "I'm using a hash set because it's O(1) lookup." A senior-level version adds the part that's easy to skip: "I'm using a hash set, which costs O(n) extra memory — if memory were tight here I'd trade that for an O(n log n) sort-based approach with no extra space, but I'm assuming memory isn't the constraint given the stated scale."

That second sentence does real work: it shows I considered an alternative and made a deliberate call, not that a hash set was the only thing I know. I also narrate more about *why I'm not* doing something — "I could add caching here but it doesn't help the worst case, so I'm skipping it for now" — because staff-level signal is partly about scope discipline, knowing what not to build under time pressure.

The other shift is pacing: at senior level I narrate less about mechanics than I used to and more about the judgment calls, because the interviewer is spending less time checking whether I *can* code and more time checking how I *reason*.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate how your own communication style has matured with seniority, which is itself a form of self-awareness signal.
